originalQuestion.prompt: What must happen before two daughter cells inherit complete copies of a chromosome?

options.text: Replicate its DNA base sequence
options.feedback: Correct. Replication precedes cell division because each daughter cell requires an inherited copy of the DNA base sequence.

options.text: Translate every gene into a protein
options.feedback: Consider why “Translate every gene into a protein” does not answer this question. Replication produces new DNA molecules; transcription produces RNA.

options.text: Break all phosphodiester bonds
options.feedback: Consider why “Break all phosphodiester bonds” does not answer this question. Replication produces new DNA molecules; transcription produces RNA.

options.text: Replace every thymine with uracil
options.feedback: Consider why “Replace every thymine with uracil” does not answer this question. Replication produces new DNA molecules; transcription produces RNA.

replacementQuestion.prompt: A cell enters mitosis without duplicating its chromosomal DNA, although it has synthesized many proteins. Which process was missing for both daughter cells to receive complete copies of the chromosomes?

options.text: Template-directed DNA replication before division
options.feedback: DNA replication produces two copies of each chromosome's sequence; subsequent chromosome segregation can then distribute one copy to each daughter cell.

options.text: Translation of every mRNA into protein
options.feedback: Translation uses ribosomes to make proteins from mRNA. Making proteins does not copy the DNA sequences that daughter cells inherit.

options.text: Breaking every phosphodiester bond in each chromosome
options.feedback: Phosphodiester bonds form the sugar–phosphate backbone. Replication separates base-paired strands without destroying the entire DNA backbone.

options.text: Replacing thymine in DNA with uracil
options.feedback: Uracil is ordinarily found in RNA; DNA replication preserves complementary DNA base pairing (A–T, C–G) rather than converting DNA to RNA.

replacementQuestion.prompt: After semi-conservative replication, each daughter DNA duplex contains which strands?

options.text: One parental and one new strand
options.feedback: Each original strand templates a new complementary strand, so each daughter DNA duplex contains one parental and one newly synthesized strand.

options.text: Two original parental strands
options.feedback: Keeping both parental strands together in one duplex describes the conservative model, not semiconservative replication.

options.text: Two unrelated DNA molecules
options.feedback: Daughter DNA is related to the parental molecule by complementary base pairing; new strands are not random unrelated molecules.

options.text: Only newly synthesized strands
options.feedback: Each daughter duplex retains one original template strand; a duplex containing only new strands is not the semiconservative outcome.

originalQuestion.prompt: What is the immediate action of helicase at a replication fork?

options.text: Separate DNA strands by disrupting base-pair hydrogen bonds
options.feedback: Correct. Helicase uses energy to unwind the parental double helix and disrupt the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, exposing the two template strands.

options.text: Join Okazaki fragments by covalent bonds
options.feedback: Consider why “Join Okazaki fragments by covalent bonds” does not answer this question. Helicase separates strands by disrupting base-pair hydrogen bonds, leaving both backbones intact.

options.text: Add amino acids to DNA
options.feedback: Consider why “Add amino acids to DNA” does not answer this question. Helicase separates strands by disrupting base-pair hydrogen bonds, leaving both backbones intact.

options.text: Replace RNA primers with DNA
options.feedback: Consider why “Replace RNA primers with DNA” does not answer this question. Helicase separates strands by disrupting base-pair hydrogen bonds, leaving both backbones intact.

replacementQuestion.prompt: What is the immediate action of helicase at a replication fork?

options.text: Separate DNA strands by disrupting base-pair hydrogen bonds
options.feedback: Helicase unwinds the parental duplex by disrupting hydrogen bonds between complementary bases; covalent sugar–phosphate backbones remain intact.

options.text: Join Okazaki fragments by covalent bonds
options.feedback: DNA ligase seals nicks in the sugar–phosphate backbone between Okazaki fragments; helicase unwinds double-stranded DNA.

options.text: Add amino acids to DNA
options.feedback: Ribosomes join amino acids during protein synthesis; helicase acts on DNA base pairs, not peptide formation.

options.text: Replace RNA primers with DNA
options.feedback: RNA primer removal and replacement involve nucleases and DNA polymerase, not helicase's strand-separation function.

originalQuestion.prompt: What links a protein-coding gene to a cellular trait?

options.text: Transcription, translation and protein function

options.text: Universal expression of every gene
options.feedback: Consider why “Universal expression of every gene” does not answer this question. Most protein-coding genes act through transcription followed by translation and protein function.

options.text: Division of every organelle
options.feedback: Consider why “Division of every organelle” does not answer this question. Most protein-coding genes act through transcription followed by translation and protein function.

replacementQuestion.prompt: Two tissues carry the same protein-coding gene but produce different amounts of its product. Which chain most directly links gene expression to a tissue-specific trait?

options.text: Regulated transcription, translation and action of the resulting protein
options.feedback: Different transcription rates can change mRNA abundance, protein production and consequently a trait, without a change in the DNA sequence.

options.text: Conversion of DNA directly into amino acids
options.feedback: DNA is transcribed to RNA, then ribosomes translate mRNA codons into a polypeptide; the DNA template does not convert directly into amino acids.

options.text: Division of every organelle
options.feedback: Organelle division is not the informational pathway from a protein-coding DNA sequence to a polypeptide and its cellular effect.

originalQuestion.prompt: If mRNA is degraded faster while transcription stays constant, what generally happens to its abundance?

options.text: It falls
options.feedback: Correct. A newly made mRNA can be translated repeatedly while it persists.

options.text: It must rise
options.feedback: Consider why “It must rise” does not answer this question. mRNA degradation regulates how long transcripts remain available for translation.

options.text: The DNA sequence changes to RNA
options.feedback: Consider why “The DNA sequence changes to RNA” does not answer this question. mRNA degradation regulates how long transcripts remain available for translation.

options.text: Every ribosome gains a new gene
options.feedback: Consider why “Every ribosome gains a new gene” does not answer this question. mRNA degradation regulates how long transcripts remain available for translation.

replacementQuestion.prompt: If mRNA is degraded faster while transcription stays constant, what generally happens to its abundance?

options.text: It falls
options.feedback: If transcripts are produced at the same rate but degraded more rapidly, their steady-state abundance normally falls and less mRNA is available for translation.

options.text: It must rise
options.feedback: Increased degradation removes transcripts faster; with transcription unchanged, it does not force the mRNA pool to grow.

options.text: The DNA sequence changes to RNA
options.feedback: Transcription uses DNA as a template to synthesize RNA; it does not change the DNA sequence into RNA. Degradation removes RNA transcripts.

options.text: Every ribosome gains a new gene
options.feedback: Ribosomes translate mRNA; they do not acquire a new gene when an mRNA molecule is degraded.

originalQuestion.prompt: What makes a typical forest an open system?

options.text: No sunlight reaches producers.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Matter cycles internally but also enters and exits ecosystems; only a closed system prevents matter exchange.

options.text: Every atom remains fixed in its original organism.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Matter cycles internally but also enters and exits ecosystems; only a closed system prevents matter exchange.

options.text: Both matter and energy cross its boundaries.
options.feedback: Correct. A closed system exchanges energy but not matter with its surroundings, while an isolated system would exchange neither; the latter is only an idealization.

options.text: Energy enters, but water and gases cannot leave.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Matter cycles internally but also enters and exits ecosystems; only a closed system prevents matter exchange.

replacementQuestion.prompt: A forest receives sunlight and rainfall, releases thermal energy and water vapour, and exchanges carbon dioxide with the atmosphere. Which property makes it an open system?

options.text: No sunlight reaches producers.
options.feedback: Sunlight is an energy input to photosynthesis, but an open system can also exchange water, gases and other matter with its surroundings.

options.text: Every atom remains fixed in its original organism.
options.feedback: Atoms move between organisms, soil, air and water; recycling within the ecosystem is compatible with exchanges across the system boundary.

options.text: Both matter and energy cross its boundaries.
options.feedback: Both matter (for example, water and CO₂) and energy (light input and heat output) cross the forest boundary.

options.text: Energy enters, but water and gases cannot leave.
options.feedback: Forest ecosystems lose water by evaporation or runoff and exchange gases. Energy-only exchange would describe a closed system, not an open one.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which statement about gametes and diploid zygotes is correct?

options.text: Gametes remain diploid throughout fertilization.
options.feedback: A diploid offspring normally receives one copy of each autosomal gene from each parent.

options.text: Gamete fusion restores the diploid complement after meiotic reduction.

options.text: The zygote receives all of its autosomes from one parent.
options.feedback: Not in this case. This alternating halving and restoration is shared by eukaryotes with sexual life cycles, although the relative duration of haploid and diploid stages differs among species.

options.text: Mitosis is the usual process that halves the chromosome number.
options.feedback: Not in this case. This alternating halving and restoration is shared by eukaryotes with sexual life cycles, although the relative duration of haploid and diploid stages differs among species.

replacementQuestion.prompt: Which statement about gametes and diploid zygotes is correct?

options.text: Gametes remain diploid throughout fertilization.
options.feedback: Gametes are typically haploid in diploid organisms. Meiosis halves the chromosome number before fertilization; gametes do not remain diploid in this cycle.

options.text: Gamete fusion restores the diploid complement after meiotic reduction.
options.feedback: Meiosis produces haploid gametes; fusion of their nuclei at fertilization restores a diploid zygote.

options.text: The zygote receives all of its autosomes from one parent.
options.feedback: For a normal diploid zygote formed by gamete fusion, one haploid chromosome set comes from each parent rather than all autosomes coming from one.

options.text: Mitosis is the usual process that halves the chromosome number.
options.feedback: Mitosis ordinarily preserves chromosome number in daughter nuclei; meiosis is the division process that reduces a diploid complement to haploid gametes.

originalQuestion.prompt: Explain genetic crosses in flowering plants using a causal mechanism and a relevant example or calculation.
originalQuestion.answer:
In a flowering plant such as a pea, pollen contains the male gametes and the embryo sac within an ovule in the ovary contains the egg cell. To make a controlled cross, a breeder prevents self-pollination of the chosen female parent, transfers pollen from the selected male parent, and labels the cross. Some flowers contain both male and female reproductive structures and can self-pollinate unless this is prevented.
Cross TT with tt pea plants: every F1 plant is Tt. Self-fertilize F1 to predict the F2 genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.

originalQuestion.prompt: Using an ecological example, explain: Why can population growth slow even when individuals still reproduce?
originalQuestion.answer: Carrying capacity, commonly denoted K, is the approximate number of individuals an environment can sustain over time under its current resource constraints. Food, water, breeding sites and suitable territory may become limiting as population size increases. Because conditions change seasonally or with disturbance, carrying capacity is not a permanent fixed species property. When individuals compete for scarce resources, per-capita survival or reproductive success may decline. That can reduce net growth before all resources are exhausted. Carrying capacity is therefore an ecosystem-dependent estimate and not a claim that the same number of individuals must be present at every moment.
markingPoints: Explain the scientific principle: Carrying capacity, commonly denoted K, is the approximate number of individuals an environment can sustain over time under its current resource constraints.
Support the explanation with relevant ecological reasoning or a valid example: On a small island, a grazing herbivore population may approach a limit set by seasonal vegetation productivity.

replacementQuestion.prompt: An isolated island population records 18 births and 16 deaths in one year, with no migration. Calculate the net change in population size and explain one reason growth can slow near carrying capacity even while births continue.

markingPoints: Calculates a net gain of 2 individuals from 18 − 16, with the correct positive sign.
Explains a density-dependent mechanism (for example resource competition reducing survival or reproduction) that lowers net growth despite ongoing births.

patches.originalIssue: Two generic explanation points with little comparative reasoning.

originalQuestion.prompt: Explain with a mechanism and a specific example: Why do autotrophs need an external energy source?
originalQuestion.answer: Autotrophs build organic carbon compounds from simple inorganic sources, especially carbon dioxide. Carbon fixation and the subsequent synthesis of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and other molecules require energy. Autotrophs therefore must capture energy from an external source rather than obtaining all carbon compounds by eating other organisms. New carbon compounds are the basis of biomass production in most ecosystems. Autotrophy is defined by where an organism obtains the carbon for biosynthesis; photosynthesis and chemosynthesis describe possible energy sources. Autotrophs also respire to provide ATP for cellular work, so they are not exempt from energy losses.
markingPoints: Identify the key process or principle: Autotrophs build organic carbon compounds from simple inorganic sources, especially carbon dioxide.
Explain its consequence or evidence, using an appropriate example: A green leaf fixes atmospheric carbon dioxide and builds sugars used later to make cellulose in growing cell walls.

A uses light energy (photoautotrophy), whereas B uses energy from oxidation of inorganic chemical substances (chemoautotrophy); carbon source and energy source are distinct classifications.
